1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Purpose of the Report
The Report presents the results of the Electricity Regulatory Authority
(ERA)’s review of the Licensees’ 2026 tariff submissions. It sets out the
approvals for the respective revenue requirements that informed
the electricity end-user tariffs for the Tariff Year 2026.
1.2 Background
Before the end of each Tariff Year, the ERA undertakes the Annual
Tariff Review for the subsequent Tariff Year. The 2026 Annual Tariff
Review was undertaken in accordance with the Electricity Act,
Cap. 157, the tariff methodologies in the respective Licences, the
Quarterly Tariff Review Adjustment Methodology, and the Electricity
(Application for Permit, Licence and Tariff Review) Regulations,
2007.
1.3 2026 Tariff Applications
1.3.1 Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited
On 1st April 2025, Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited
(UEGCL) submitted its application for renewal of the Nalubaale and
Kiira Generation Complex and tariff performance parameters
under the Multi-Year Tariff (MYT) application for the period 2026 to
2028. The application included tariff performance parameters for
the for the period January to December 2026.
1.3.2 Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited
On 1st August 2025, Uganda Electricity Transmission Company
Limited (UETCL) submitted its application for the renewal of the
licences issued to the company and tariff performance parameters
for Transmission Operation and Maintenance Costs, Capital, and
the non-grid budget for the period 2026 to 2030. Additionally, in
November 2025, UETCL submitted the demand and dispatch
forecasts for Tariff Year 2026.

1.4 The Tariff Review Process
The tariff review process commenced with the publication of the
applications in the New Vision newspaper dated 10th November
2025. Key stakeholders and the general public were invited to view
the applications and submit their comments and representations
regarding the Tariff Applications. During the 15-day notice period,
the applications were available for public scrutiny on the ERA
website, at the ERA Resource Centre, and at the ERA Regional
Offices in Mbale, Mbarara, and Gulu.
On 27th November 2025, the ERA published a notice inviting key
stakeholders and the general public to a Public
Hearing/Consultation regarding the 2026 Tariff Applications. The
Public Hearing was held on 9th December 2025 in Kampala City and
simultaneously online during which the licensees presented their
2026 Tariff Applications.
As part of the 2026 tariff review, the Authority undertook additional
stakeholder consultations with the Ministry of Finance, Planning and
Economic Development (MoFPED), the Ministry of Energy and
Mineral Development (MEMD), the Uganda Manufacturers

In determining the 2026 base tariffs, the Authority considered the

1.5 Major Assumptions for the 2026 Tariff Review
The 2026 annual tariff review was undertaken in consideration of
the following major factors/assumptions:
(i) Electricity demand is expected to grow at an annual rate of
approximately 14.51% in 2026. The total energy purchased by
UETCL is expected to increase from 8,019.8 GWh projected
for 2025 to 9,183.4 GWh in 2026;
(ii) The Authority issued two Licences for the Distribution and Sale
of Electricity to the UEDCL. The UEDCL Licence for Sale of
Electricity provides for a Tariff Methodology to guide the
determination of the Retail Tariff effective April 2025;
(iii) The Authority will implement the Quarterly Tariff Adjustment
Methodology in Tariff Year 2026. The Quarterly Tariff
Adjustment Methodology, implemented by the Authority
since 2014 and in the subsequent tariff years, adjusts the
annual base tariff for changes in inflation, exchange rate,
price of fuel on the international market, and other costs
approved by the Authority;
(iv) The Government of Uganda (GOU) will continue paying
capacity payments to the thermal plants (Namanve and
Electro-Maxx) in 2026 and debt service to the UEB successor
companies (UEGCL, UETCL, and UEDCL). As such, these costs
will not be financed through the electricity tariff;

2 ELECTRICITY DEMAND
2.1 Maximum Demand
A review was conducted on the power system summaries reported
by UETCL from November 2024 to October 2025. The system
(including exports to Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda) registered a
maximum peak demand of 1,335.80 MW in September 2025
compared to 1,095.98 MW in November 2024. This peak demand
movement represents a 21.8% increase. In addition, the maximum
domestic (Ugandan) peak demand was 1,157.24 MW in September
2025 compared to 944.57 MW in November 2024, representing a
22.5% increase in national peak demand.
The increase in demand is mainly attributed to the connection of
new large customers, specifically data centres, and to the general
resilience of the Ugandan economy against external shocks but at
the same time bolstered by slight improvement in global growth.
Prudent monetary policy and targeted fiscal measures have
maintained macroeconomic stability and reinforced investor
confidence.
During the year, the Authority also noted increased exports to
Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. Total exports have increased from
734 MW in October 2024 to 980.86 MW in October 2025,
representing a 33.6% increase.

2.2 Uganda’s Economic Performance
The Bank of Uganda maintained the Central Bank Rate (CBR) at
9.75% as reported in its Monetary Policy Statement for November
2025. The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth reached 6.3
percent in FY 2024/25, up from 6.1 percent in the previous year,
supported by improvements in agricultural and industrial activities.
The economy is expected to keep the expansion trajectory up to
between 6.5 percent and 7 percent in FY 2025/26. This reflects
sustained economic resilience, arising from a slight improvement in
global growth, prudent monetary policy and targeted fiscal

reinforced investor confidence. Growth is also being supported by
the ongoing large-scale infrastructure investments, sustained
private investment and the implementation of the Tenfold Growth
Strategy, which is unlocking opportunities in agriculture,
infrastructure, and the extractive industries.
The inflation outlook has been revised slightly downward relative to
the August 2025 forecast. Core inflation is now projected to range
between 4 percent and 4.5 percent, compared to 4.5 percent and
4.8 percent in the previous forecast for FY 2025/26, which remains
below the 5 percent target over the next 12 months.
2.3 Measures to Increase the Demand for Electricity
2.3.1 Development of Regional Industrial Parks
The Government of Uganda, through the Uganda Investment
Authority (UIA), is fast-tracking the development of regional
industrial parks. During the Tariff Year 2024, UETCL, in partnership with
the Development Partners and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral
Development, commissioned the Olwiyo – Nebbi – Arua
transmission line and the associated substations, in addition to the
completion of Tororo – Lira – Kole – Gulu and Achwa lines and the
associated substations.
In 2025, UETCL also commissioned the 132 kV Mirama – Kabale
transmission line and its associated substations. The commissioned
substations are expected to improve power reliability in the greater
North, West Nile, and Kigezi Regions, thereby increasing energy
demand. The connection of West Nile to the national grid is also
expected to increase demand in 2026, as the region takes
advantage of the reliable supply from the National Grid.
2.3.2 Household Electrification
The Authority has continued to implement the hybrid connection
framework following full utilization of the Uganda Development
Bank loan contribution.

Access Scale-up Project (EASP). This loan and grant facility is
expected to connect over one (1) million households, both no-pole
and one-pole. The EASP development objective is to increase
access to energy for households, commercial enterprises, industrial
parks, and public institutions.
2.3.3 Regional Power Trading
As of October 2025, the registered average maximum net exports
to Tanzania, Kenya and Rwanda stood at 35.36 MW, 105.53 MW
and 63.93 MW, respectively. There is also export potential to
countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo and South
Sudan, subject to construction of interconnections with these
countries. Additionally, the East African Power Pool is expected to
launch its day ahead market in the year 2026. With the existing
interconnectors, Uganda will be poised to participate in the
regional power pool.
3 GENERATION ASSUMPTIONS
3.1 International Oil Price Assumptions
In the 2025 Base Tariffs, the cost of crude oil assumed in the tariff
determination was USD 79.38 per barrel, translating into USD 592.17
per metric ton of Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO). During the 2025 Tariff Year,
international oil prices have generally decreased compared to the
previous Tariff Year, driven by fears of oversupply, easing of
demand and the geopolitical tensions.
According to the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries
(OPEC), as of the end of November 2025, the price of oil on the
international market, proxied by the cost of the reference basket
for crude oil, was USD 64.46 per barrel, an 18.8% reduction from
November 2024.
OPEC+ and non-OPEC producers are increasing output through
investments in new capacity, signaling planned production

3.2 Energy Purchases by UETCL
By the end of 2025, total demand was expected to grow by 20%.
This was attributed to the expansion of the economy, with the GDP
growing by 6.3% and the connection of data centres to the
national grid, thus driving domestic demand. This was coupled by
the growing exports to the region, altogether contributing to the
growth in the overall system demand.
In 2026, UETCL is expected to purchase a total of 9,183.4 GWh from
all generation plants and imports. The projection for 2026 envisages
a growth of 14.51% from the annualized purchases of 8,019.8 GWh
in 2025. This is attributed to the envisaged growth trajectory in the
economic activities at the macro level, demand growth by more
large power users (data centres) connected to the grid, industrial
activities, take off of huge oil production activities, the roll-out of
EASP, and increased export opportunities to Rwanda, Kenya and
Tanzania.
3.3 Energy Purchases by UETCL from the Generation Power Plants
Based on the capacity, plants along the River Nile are expected to
balance the system demand and supply in consideration of the
regulated water limits, which have an impact on the expected
dispatch from the large hydro power plants such as Karuma Hydro
Power Plant (HPP).
Mandatory dispatch is expected on the other plants, considering
the respective Power Purchase Agreements (PPA) and the

3.3.1 Large Hydro Power Plants
3.3.1.1 Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro Power Plants (380 MW)
The Authority approved the renewal of the Licence for Generation
and Sale of electricity issued to UEGCL for a period of three (3) years
effective January 2026. The Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro Complex
has an installed capacity of 380 MW. In 2026, this facility will be
dispatched at an average of 189.92 MW, translating into
annualized energy of 1,663.7 GWh. The dispatch levels from the
Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro Power Complex are expected to affect
the dispatch of other power plants along the River Nile.
The annualized power purchase costs for Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro
Power Complex are expected to increase from USh 77.07 billion in
2025 to USh 90.47 billion in 2026. The increase in the annualized
power purchase costs is attributed to the revision of the tariff
performance parameters.
3.3.1.2 Bujagali Hydro Power Plant (250 MW)
The generation of electricity from the 250 MW Bujagali HPP is a
function of the water release from the Nalubaale and Kiira Hydro
Power Complex, which is limited to 1,000 cumecs by the Directorate
of Water Resources Management. Considering the routine plant
maintenance schedule per year and expected water release,
Bujagali HPP is projected to generate at an average capacity of
193.51 MW, translating into annualized energy of 1,695.1 GWh for
the Tariff Year 2026.
The annualized power purchase costs for Bujagali Energy Limited
are expected to increase from USh 435.62 billion in 2025 to USh
446.04 billion in the Tariff Year 2026. The increase in power purchase

3.3.1.3 Isimba Hydro Power Plant (183 MW)
The 183 MW Isimba Hydro Power Plant is expected to have an
average of 121.4 MW available for dispatch in 2026 based on
installed capacity and the designed plant factor. The plant is
expected to undergo major maintenance, which will affect its
operations in the Tariff Year 2026.
Despite the scheduled maintenance, the plant is planned to
operate at an average capacity of 121.4 MW. Based on the
demand-supply forecast, UETCL is expected to dispatch annualized
energy of 1,063.43 GWh from Isimba HPP in 2026.
According to the Licence for Isimba, the plant is contracted at an
energy charge of US cents 4.16/kWh for the first ten (10) years after
the commissioning of the project. This generation tariff is subject to
adjustment for changes in the US Producer Price Index (US PPI). In
accordance with the generation tariff adjustment formula, the
energy tariff applicable to Isimba HPP for the Tariff Year 2026 is US
cents 4.353 per kWh.
The power purchase costs for Isimba HPP are expected to increase
from USh 157.48 billion in 2025 to USh 167.80 billion in 2026. The
projected increase in power purchase costs in 2026 is due
to depreciation of the Uganda Shilling against the United States
Dollar and to the adjustment of the generation tariff as per the tariff
methodology in the Licence.

3.3.1.4 Karuma Hydro Power Plant (600 MW)
In 2026, the 600 MW Karuma Hydro Power Plant is expected to
generate an average capacity of 258.27 MW, translating into
annualised energy generation of 2,262.4 GWh.
According to the Licence for Karuma, the Plant is contracted at an
energy charge of US cents 4.97 per kWh for the first ten years of the
